name: TPU 95A (standard flexible)
chemical_makeup: Thermoplastic polyurethane at Shore 95A — the highest hard-segment ratio of the Shore A filament grades, giving firm-rubber behaviour. Reference products are NinjaTek Cheetah 95A and Polymaker PolyFlex TPU95
summary: The industry-standard flexible and the grade most people mean when they say 'TPU': firm shoe-sole feel, the best balance of flexibility against printability in the Shore A family. Delta vs base TPU: this is the firm end of the base entry's 85A-95A band and is where its caveats relax — speed climbs to 25-45 mm/s, limited retraction of 0.5-2 mm works, and a short well-constrained Bowden path is survivable, so drive_system is recorded as recommended rather than required. Still barred from the AMS, and still the best-documented grade for actual numbers.

printing.notes: Brand windows: Polymaker PolyFlex TPU95 210-230 °C on a 25-60 °C plate, NinjaTek Cheetah 225-250 °C — the recorded 210-250 °C range spans both. Bed 50-60 °C gives the best adhesion though room temperature works. Speed 25-45 mm/s is the fastest of the common Shore A grades and roughly triple what 60A tolerates; many tuned direct-drive machines run this grade without extensive profile work. Limited retraction of 0.5-2 mm is usable, unlike the softer grades that need it off. No enclosure required; on an enclosed printer run with the lid open as for base TPU. Not abrasive — standard brass nozzle.

feeding.notes: The one grade in the family where Bowden is not an automatic no: community consensus is that a well-tuned short Bowden path can limp 95A through at low speed, though it is not reliable and direct drive remains strongly preferred. This is the specific case the base entry describes when it records direct-drive-required for the 85A-95A range as a whole while noting 95A's short-Bowden tolerance — here it is recorded as 'recommended' rather than 'required'. AMS is still no: Bambu places 95A in the 'moderately hard' bucket with 85A/83A/80A, printable directly on its printers but liable to bend and cause feeding failures inside a material station. A spool-side feeding assistant is unnecessary at this durometer.

methods: dedicated filament dryer at 70 °C for 8 h
print directly from a drybox with desiccant
drying.dryness_validation: No popping or crackling at the nozzle, no foamy or bubbly extrudate, and no rise in stringing on a retraction test — this last check is genuinely usable at 95A, unlike the softer grades that string when dry
drying.notes: Polymaker specifies 70 °C for 8 h for PolyFlex TPU95, consistent with the general TPU regime and with the base entry. Hardness does not shift the drying window; what differs is tolerance — 95A survives a skipped drying cycle more often than the softer grades, though the base entry's 'always' still applies.

storage.recommendations: Sealed with desiccant under 20% RH. The most forgiving grade in the family for open-air exposure, but a damp spool still prints with popping and rough surfaces, so keep the drybox habit.

price.notes: Polymaker PolyFlex TPU95 at $29.99 per 0.75 kg works out to about $40/kg. NinjaTek Cheetah 95A and the near-sibling Fillamentum Flexfill 92A sit in a $40-70/kg band across retailers, exact per-kg figures unverified. Cheaper than 85A/90A because 95A is the volume grade every brand stocks; the base entry's $20-25 budget-generic floor is plausible for no-name 95A but was not confirmed by these sources.

recommended: general-purpose flexible parts where no specific durometer is called for

properties.notes: The best-documented grade in the family. NinjaTek Cheetah 95A: density 1.22 g/cm³, tensile yield 9 MPa and ultimate 39 MPa, elongation 55% at yield and 580% at break. Polymaker PolyFlex TPU95: density 1.20-1.24 g/cm³, 25.8±0.4 MPa at 400% strain, elongation at break 551.2±23.5%. Fillamentum Flexfill 92A (near sibling): density 1.20 g/cm³, tensile 49 MPa on a differing test basis, likely ultimate. Density of 1.22 is the NinjaTek figure and coincides with the base entry's recorded value. Elongation of roughly 550-580% is dramatically below tpu-60a's ~950%, and tensile correspondingly higher — the clearest quantitative statement of the stiffness-for-stretch trade across the Shore A grades. Max service temperature of 72 °C is an unverified estimate, marginally above the base entry's 70 °C because this is the firmest A-grade.

compatibility.notes: Welds to base TPU and all sibling grades — the usual multi-durometer pattern is a 95A structural body with 60A or 85A soft zones. Bonding to rigid materials is unchanged from the base entry: PLA and PETG joints rely on mechanical interlock, with PETG the more reliable of the two; no useful bond to ABS, ASA, PC or PA. PLA is the practical breakaway support because it releases cleanly; PVA and HIPS are not documented as reliable TPU interfaces.

plate_recommendations.notes: Textured PEI is the default for this grade and works well from room temperature to a 60 °C bed, per community consensus and Bambu's plate compatibility notes. Over-adhesion is still the failure mode rather than lifting, but 95A is firm enough that parts usually release without tearing — the reason this grade rates 'recommended' where the softer siblings rate 'usable'.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): As base TPU; the hardest grade and the easiest case.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Firmer TPU grades release cleanly; the low-fusing behavior is the main reason flexible printers pick G10 over PEI.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Firmer grades release readily by flexing the steel backing.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): The hardest common grade and the most survivable on smooth PEI, but still needs a separator.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Firmer grades peel off a rigid plate more easily than soft ones, which want to stretch rather than release.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Hardest common grade; still follow the glue-stick guidance.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Hardest common grade; the most predictable of the TPUs here.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): The hardest common grade and the one most often attempted anyway; still covered by the blanket TPU warning.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Firmer grades are no exception; use a textured PEI, G10 or carbon plate for flexibles.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): The hardest common grade and the least bad case, but still inside the vendor's fusion warning.

emissions.notes: Standard TPU-family profile as recorded in the base entry — moderate ultrafine particles, some VOCs including possible isocyanates, minimal styrene. No source differentiates emissions by Shore grade (unverified). Brand nozzle windows for this grade reach 250 °C (NinjaTek Cheetah), and emissions rise with nozzle temperature, so ventilation matters more when running the top of the range than the 210 °C bottom.

safety_notes: Urethane chemistry can in principle release isocyanate residues at print temperature; NinjaTek's 250 °C ceiling is the point where thermal decomposition becomes more likely, so favour the lower half of the window unless flow demands otherwise. Not food-contact certified as printed — verify per SKU.
additional_notes: Anisotropy is the design constraint inherited from the base entry: Z strength is roughly four times lower than XY across TPU, so orient parts so stretching and bending load layers in-plane. Elastic recovery also means printed dimensions settle slightly off nominal, which rules this grade out for press fits held to tight tolerance even though it is the most dimensionally stable of the Shore A grades.

provenance.conflicts: Tensile figures are not directly comparable across sources because the test bases differ: NinjaTek reports 39 MPa ultimate, Polymaker 25.8 MPa at 400% strain (a stress-at-strain figure, not ultimate), Fillamentum 49 MPa on an unstated basis — the recorded 25-49 MPa range spans all three rather than pretending they measure the same thing. Nozzle temperature disagrees by 40 °C between Polymaker (210-230) and NinjaTek (225-250). Density spans 1.20-1.24 across the same three brands. Drive system is recorded as 'recommended' where the base entry records 'required' for the range; this is a deliberate grade-level relaxation based on community reports of short-Bowden success, not a datasheet claim. Max service temperature is unverified. Scoring note: the research notes rated 'compression recovery' 6/10 here, but this catalog's compression_strength score measures resistance to crushing loads, which is the inverse — 95A scores 3, above the softer siblings for exactly the reason it recovers less.
